citations.excerpt: A religious movement which was originated in 1739 by John Wesley in the Anglican Church , and subsequently gave rise to numerous separate denominations .
In 1739 Wesley organized the first Methodist Society, laid the foundation of the first separate place of worship at Bristol

facts.value_before_verify: 1739, first Methodist society. Oxford group from 1729

citations.excerpt: originated in 1739 by John Wesley in the Anglican Church

facts.value: John Wesley, with Charles Wesley and George Whitefield

citations.locator: Methodism (J. C. A. Voelcker and J. M. Buckley)
citations.excerpt: denoting the religious organizations which trace their origin to the evangelistic teaching of John Wesley.
As the pulpits of the Established Church were closed against the Wesleys and Whitefield, the latter took the decisive step of preaching in the open air

facts.value: Personal religion and the immediate work of the Holy Spirit, aiming "to spread Scriptural holiness over the land." Doctrinal standards are Wesley's Notes on the New Testament and his Sermons.

citations.excerpt: Methodism began in a revival of personal religion, and it professed to have but one aim, viz. “to spread Scriptural holiness over the land.”
standards of Methodist doctrine are laid down as consisting of “Mr Wesley’s Notes on the New Testament and the 1st Series of his Sermons”

facts.value: A revival movement within the Church of England. Wesley organized his followers into societies and, finding Anglican churches closed to them, preached in the open air. The main British streams came together as the Methodist Church in 1932.

citations.excerpt: Wesley and his helpers, finding the Anglican churches closed against them, took to preaching in the open air
The main streams of Methodism came together as "The Methodist Church" in 1932.

citations.locator: Methodism (J. C. A. Voelcker and J. M. Buckley)
citations.excerpt: when John Wesley had organized his followers into “societies” the name was applied to them in the same spirit.

facts.value_before_verify: A revival movement within the Church of England that organized followers into societies with lay preachers and open-air preaching, and later formed separate churches. The main British streams reunited as the Methodist Church in 1932.
